applies_why: The text decides a link-versus-link collision (D6 vs C1) by weighing the challenger's chain against the defender's chain as wholes, which is exactly the chain-against-chain collision K-C governs.
quote: the challenger's seed/loins chain is footed but does not name Joseph as the begetter; the defender's chain is footed but rests on the woman-route inference
rule_words: the collision weighs chain against chain by footing, never verse by verse; that no one of them states the contrary in its own words is the stating-verse test DG-61 retires, at a judge's seat as at a debater's, for either side / A link is judged by its support, never by whether any verse, or the chain as a whole, states it word for word
room: Rule phrase 'that no one of them states the contrary in its own words' applied to the judge's 'does not name Joseph as the begetter': reading A — a statement-absence discount, the chain already pronounced footed being marked down because neither any verse nor the chain as a whole names Joseph as begetter, the retired stating-verse test in use; reading B — a footing note, the chain's support merely stopping short of the Joseph-as-begetter step. I chose A because 'name' is statement language set as a 'but' after footing was granted, and the twin 'rests on the woman-route inference' likewise faults the defender's footed chain for being inferential rather than stated — the same statement-over-support demand on both sides.
why: Having granted both chains footing, the judge let the collision turn on the absence of explicit statement — no naming of Joseph as begetter on one side, mere inference on the other — which is the stating-verse test DG-61 retires at a judge's seat, not a weighing chain against chain by footing.
